planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Lemon Lime holds its bright striping best with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Lemon Lime produces long, arching, strap-like leaves striped lengthwise in bright chartreuse-yellow and two shades of green, giving a bold, sunny color effect even in a dim interior corner where its glow of yellow reads as light. It grows as a tall, cane-forming plant over years, developing a trunk-like base with tufts of foliage similar to other corn plant dracaenas, and tolerates the low humidity and inconsistent watering typical of home and office environments. Water when the top inch or two of potting mix dries out, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and wipe dust from the leaves periodically to keep them looking their brightest.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light to open shade in well-drained potting mix; Florida Beauty tolerates lower light than most other variegated dracaenas.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light to open shade in well-drained potting mix. Florida Beauty is a slender, wiry-stemmed dracaena with narrow, dark green leaves densely speckled in creamy yellow-gold spots, giving each leaf a scattered, gold-dust appearance quite different from the broad, solid, or striped leaves of most other dracaena cultivars. Its more delicate, cane-like stems and smaller leaf size suit it to a tabletop or shelf as readily as a larger floor specimen, and it branches and fills out over time to form a bushier, more textural plant than upright corn plant types. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and mist occasionally or provide a pebble tray, since this species appreciates slightly higher humidity than some other dracaenas.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Colorama holds its pink striping best with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Colorama is the most vividly colored form of the classic dragon tree, with narrow, arching leaves edged in broad bands of pink and cream over a dark green center stripe, giving it noticeably more pink than the standard 'Tricolor' cultivar it sports from. It develops the same slow-growing, sculptural, multi-trunked silhouette as other Dracaena marginata forms over years, making it a long-lived architectural floor plant. Water when the top inch or two of potting mix dries out, since dracaenas are prone to root rot in constantly wet soil, avoid fluoridated water when possible to prevent leaf-tip browning, and keep away from cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Audrey ficus wants more consistent light than a standard rubber tree and drops leaves readily if moved or under-lit.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix, positioning it where it will not need to be moved often. Audrey is the common houseplant form of the Indian banyan fig, with slightly fuzzy, matte, deep green leaves marked by pale, prominent veining, giving it a softer texture than the glossy leaves of a standard rubber tree or fiddle-leaf fig. In its native range this species grows into one of the largest-canopied trees in the world, and even as a container plant it develops real trunk and structure over years, making it a substantial architectural floor specimen. It is sensitive to being moved or rotated and to sudden drops in light, both of which can trigger leaf drop, so choose a bright spot and leave it undisturbed. Water when the top inch or two of potting mix dries, and wipe dust from the leaves periodically to keep pores clear.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Ruby holds its pink coloring best with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Ruby is a compact-growing rubber tree cultivar with glossy leaves splashed in pink, cream, and shades of green, carrying even more pink than the similar Tineke cultivar, especially on new growth, which unfurls from a bright red protective sheath. Its slightly smaller stature compared to standard green rubber trees makes it manageable in a room with limited ceiling height, while still developing into a substantial floor plant over years. Wipe dust from the large leaves periodically to keep pores clear, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and rotate the pot occasionally for even growth on all sides.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Alii ficus drops fewer leaves after a location change than most other ficus species, making it a more forgiving choice for an indoor floor plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Alii produces long, narrow, glossy, dark green, willow-like leaves that hang gracefully from slender branches, giving it a softer, more relaxed silhouette than the broad-leaved rubber tree or the finicky fiddle-leaf fig, while still forming a substantial upright floor plant over time. It tends to tolerate typical indoor conditions and minor location changes better than most other ficus species, which are notorious for dropping leaves in protest at any disruption, making Alii a comparatively low-stress choice for a tall architectural houseplant. Water when the top inch or two of potting mix dries out, wipe dust from the leaves periodically, and prune to control height and encourage fuller branching.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; White Butterfly is frost-tender outside zones 10-11 and tolerates lower light better than more heavily variegated syngonium cultivars.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. White Butterfly is one of the most popular and widely available syngonium cultivars, with arrow-shaped leaves showing a soft, pale green to creamy white center fading into green margins and veins, giving each leaf a moth-like or butterfly-like two-toned pattern that also gives the plant its common name. It grows as a bushy, upright juvenile plant before eventually developing a climbing habit with larger, more deeply lobed leaves if given a moss pole or trellis to grip. Its moderate variegation makes it noticeably tougher and more tolerant of average indoor light than heavily pink or white cultivars, and pinching growing tips keeps it compact and full. Note that, like other syngoniums, its sap can irritate skin and is toxic if chewed by pets.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Confetti colors most vividly with bright indirect light and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Confetti carries irregular flecks and splashes of pink and cream scattered across each green, arrow-shaped leaf, as though the foliage had been spattered with paint, giving it a busier, more speckled look than the cleaner center-variegated syngonium cultivars. Young plants hold a compact, bushy, upright form and can later be trained onto a moss pole or trellis, where mature leaves develop deeper lobes typical of adult syngonium growth. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the plant full and bushy rather than leggy, and provide bright indirect light for the best pink speckling, since low light causes the variegation to fade toward plain green. As with other syngoniums, the sap can irritate skin and is toxic if chewed by pets.
